newsitem.title: UK: Bond market charts darken as bears turn on Europe.
newsitem.headline: Bond market charts darken as bears turn on Europe.

text.p: Bond investors have nowhere to hide -- at least as far as the charts are concerned.
Technical signals in both the U.S. and Europe have become gloomier and analysts said on Tuesday a further round of declines was in the offing.
Against a background of inflation and interest rate worries in the U.S., Treasuries have been battered in recent weeks. European debt had generally outperformed. Until recently.
"The sentiment has clearly changed." said David Sneddon, technical analyst at Creedit Suisse First Boston in London.

Bund futures tumbled nearly a point and a half on Monday and fell further on Tuesday. By 1335 GMT they were at 100.05, down 36 basis points from the prior close. They have shed more than three full points since late February.
"Yesterday, the pace of the move has injected some more nervousness into the market," Sneddon said.
Meanwhile in the U.S. there are growing expectations that long bond yields will rise well above seven percent, eventually taking T-bond futures into dangerous territory around 106-00.

In the past month U.S. T-bond futures have lost more than five full points and they are now trading at their lowest levels since October 1996. At 1335 GMT the June contract was at 108-16, down 8/32 from the prior close in Chicago.

The big threat is that they fall all the way to the 106-00 area, where the market bottomed out on continuation charts in June, July and September last year. That, say some, would spell serious trouble and possibly send T-bonds toward 100-00.
For now, analysts do not see a sudden drop-off either in the U.S. or Europe. But they say that even if the markets consolidate, it could be evidence of topping patterns.
"You're looking to see them at the moment consolidate in broad ranges as the market makes up its mind," Sneddon said.
"The markets technically do not look good," said London-based technical analyst Miranda Churchill. But she added, "For the moment to look for a big, big downmove is premature."
Sneddon equated supports just above the 99.00 area on June Bund futures with the 106-00 area for T-bonds.
Churchill said the recent downturn by Bunds showed they were simply playing catch-up with Treasuries.
"It's just a matter of evening things out a bit."
She said there was no sign, at least looking at the 10-year U.S./German yield spread, that the U.S. would start to outperform Germany in a major way longer-term.

While Churchill said she did not chart the spread specifically, it would have to get below 70 basis points before it looked like Bunds were in for a period of underperformance. The gap of U.S. yields over German is currently 95 basis points.
In any case, many investors are holding out for higher yields in both markets.
Donna Liu, technical analyst at DKB International, said long bond yields were near important long-term levels.
"If the yield is above 6.90 percent at month-end I'd say the trend (in yields) is upwards," she told Reuters Financial Television. Yields will initially rise to 7.25 and then 7.50 percent, she said.
And in Europe, fundamentalists said the whole debate about monetary union is beginning to make investors wary of European debt.

This has had the biggest impact on Italian debt -- which was the fastest riser when there was more optimism about a single currency -- but investor dissatisfaction is in evidence throughout Europe, they said.
